scenes.text: Last time, we opened up a eukaryotic cell and gave every organelle a job. Here are two of them side by side: a cell from a leaf, and a cell from an animal. Most of the parts match. But the leaf cell is boxy and green, and the animal cell is round and soft. Is that just a quirk, or could you predict it from what each cell has to do?

Here's a clue. Forget to water a pot plant, and it droops. Water it, and often within a few hours it stands up again. A plant has no bones and no muscles, so what's holding it up? The answer is sitting inside its cells.

Start with what they share. Plant and animal cells are both eukaryotic, so both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. Both have mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum and a Golgi body. That's the shared toolkit. The differences are a short list: the leaf cell adds a cell wall, chloroplasts and one large central vacuole. So why exactly those three?

Look at how each organism lives. A plant is an autotroph, which means it makes its own food, using light energy. It's also fixed in one spot, and it has no skeleton to hold it up. An animal is a heterotroph: it gets its food by eating other living things. It moves around, and many animals are held up by a skeleton. Every difference we're about to see follows from those two ways of life.

First job: make food. To make glucose, a leaf cell has to capture light energy, and that happens in chloroplasts. Inside each one, stacks of membranes hold a green pigment, chlorophyll, which absorbs the light. That's photosynthesis, and it's why leaves are green. An animal cell has no chloroplasts, because an animal gets its glucose already made, from food.
So here's a prediction for you. This cell comes from a root, deep underground. It's still a plant cell. Does it have chloroplasts? Have a think.

No, it doesn't. There's no light down there to capture, so chloroplasts wouldn't help. But it still has a wall and a large vacuole, because it still needs support. Even within one plant, each cell stocks the parts its own job needs. That's called structure follows function.

Second job: hold itself up without a skeleton. This is where the cell wall and the vacuole work as a team. The cell wall is a rigid layer of cellulose, tough fibres built from sugar, outside the membrane. The large central vacuole is a sac of watery cell sap that also stores nutrients and wastes. When the vacuole is full, it presses the cell outwards against the wall, and the wall pushes back, so the cell becomes firm instead of bursting. That outward push is called turgor pressure. Millions of firm cells pressing on each other hold a leaf up.

Now you can answer the pot plant puzzle. When the soil dries out, the vacuoles lose water. They stop pressing on the walls, turgor falls, and the cells go soft. Soft cells can't hold the leaves out, so the plant droops. Water it, the vacuoles refill, turgor returns, and the plant stands back up.

Now flip to the animal cell. With no wall, its outer boundary is the flexible cell membrane, so the cell can change shape. Watch this white blood cell. It flows around a bacterium, wraps it up and pulls it inside. A cell with a rigid wall couldn't do that. Animal cells have only small, temporary vacuoles, if any. And many animal cells have lysosomes, small sacs of digestive enzymes.

Here's a common trap. Plants make glucose in chloroplasts, so do plant cells need mitochondria? Yes, they do. Making glucose stores energy. To use that energy, a plant cell respires the glucose in its mitochondria, just like an animal cell. And respiration runs day and night, while photosynthesis stops in the dark. One way to remember it: a plant cell runs a kitchen and a furnace, and only the kitchen closes at night.

So what does an exam mean by contrast, based on the function of the cell? Contrast means differences, stated for both cells. And based on function means every difference needs its reason. Plant cells have a cellulose wall, animal cells don't, because the plant relies on turgor for support. Green plant cells have chloroplasts, animal cells don't, because the plant makes its own food. Plant cells have one large central vacuole, animal cells have small ones, because that vacuole stores sap and keeps turgor up.

Two exam questions. First. A cell has a nucleus, mitochondria, a cellulose cell wall and a large central vacuole, but no chloroplasts. Identify the type of cell, and justify your answer. Then explain why this cell may have no chloroplasts, yet still needs mitochondria. Pause here to answer.

It's a plant cell, because only plant cells have a cellulose wall and a large central vacuole. It probably comes from a part of the plant that gets no light, like a root, so chloroplasts wouldn't help. It still needs mitochondria, because it must respire sugars sent from the leaves to release energy. The classic mistake is saying no chloroplasts means an animal cell.
Second. A student says, plant and animal cells differ only because plants are green. Assess this statement, by contrasting the two cell types based on the function of each cell. Pause here to answer.

The statement is too narrow. Chloroplasts are one difference, there because the plant makes its own food. But plant cells also have a cellulose wall and a large central vacuole, because a plant has no skeleton and relies on turgor to stay upright. Animal cells have none of these three. Structure follows function. The classic mistake is listing differences with no reasons.

So to contrast any two cells, ask what each cell has to do, then look for the structure that does that job. Next, we visit a cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles at all. How does a bacterium stay alive?
